description: Solo participant from South Korea joining Sapporo online. Computer science student focused on backend, data, and web development. We are building a "trend detective" web tool that lets students and the public pick NASA Earth science variables (snow depth, snowfall, temperature, precipitation), see how they change over time in a region such as Hokkaido, and test whether the change is statistically significant (Mann-Kendall, Sen's slope, confidence intervals).
summary: Hokkaido is famous for light, dry snow. We asked: is it turning into heavy, wet snow? We counted every snow day of 35 winters (1992–2026) with NASA POWER daily data and 10 Japan Meteorological Agency stations, and checked the results with NASA MODIS satellite snow cover and JAXA GSMaP satellite precipitation. Heavy-snow days rose at all 10 stations and in 15 of 43 NASA cells, with none falling significantly. The snow itself got heavier: the snow that piles up from 1 mm of water fell at 9 of 10 stations, so 1 m of new snow on a Sapporo roof now weighs about 17% more. Wet heavy storms rose and April snow cover shrank by 13 points per decade. Warmer, wetter winters explain about two thirds of the change, and the places already near −3 °C changed most. Light-snow days lean down but are not yet certain, and we say so. The result is a phone web app with a 3D globe: click anywhere on Earth or search any place in any language to see its snow-quality chart, a 7-day forecast that flags fall-risk days, a timeline from 1992 to ten years ahead with what becomes more or less likely there, and open data for city snow planning.
details:
Japanese presentation slides (for the Sapporo local judging): https://hitori839.github.io/snow-trend-detective/demo/Snow_Trend_Detective_happyo_ja.pdf

What it does

My Town Snow-Quality Chart turns 35 winters of Earth observation into a chart for the place you live. Click anywhere on a 3D Earth (NASA Blue Marble), use your location, or search any place in Japanese, English, Korean or other languages. The app shows how the quality of snow there has changed, how sure we are, why it changed, what it means, and what to do this week.

The question and how we measure it

Snow quality is set by the temperature it falls in. On a snow day we call snow light when the daily mean is −5 °C or colder and heavy when it is warmer than −2 °C; new-snow density is known to rise steeply with air temperature (e.g. Hedstrom & Pomeroy 1998). Because this is a rule of thumb, we (1) re-ran the analysis with the heavy-snow cut-off at −3, −2, −1 and 0 °C — the conclusion did not change — and (2) measured weight directly: centimetres of new snow (JMA) per millimetre of water (JAXA GSMaP).

What we found (winters Dec–Mar, 1992–2026)

- Heavy-snow days rose at 10 of 10 JMA stations (3 significant) and significantly in 15 of 43 NASA ~50 km cells, with 0 significant falls. The chance of this many cells lining up by chance is 1.2 % (500-run shuffle test that keeps spatial correlation); 7 cells survive Benjamini–Hochberg FDR.

- The snow itself got heavier: snow per mm of water fell at 9 of 10 stations (5 significant, 2001–2026). Niseko went from 2.74 to 1.96 cm/mm. The roof load of 1 m of new snow in Sapporo rose from about 55 to 64 kg/m².

- Quantity vs quality: the amount of snow barely changed (snow days show no clear trend; Sapporo 64 → 64 days) — its quality did.

- Wet heavy storms (≥ 10 mm/day of JAXA precipitation at a mean above −2 °C) rose at 10 of 10 stations; Sapporo 3.2 → 4.6 days per winter (p = 0.02).

- Icy-road days (thaw by day, freeze at night) rose significantly in 15 of 43 cells (chance 2 %).

- April snow cover seen by NASA MODIS fell by 13.1 percentage points per decade across Hokkaido (p = 0.003); all 42 cells fell, 30 significantly.

- Why: winters warmed 0.3 °C per decade (all 43 cells up; all 10 stations significant, rural towns as much as Sapporo, so not just urban heat). Warming alone explains about 46 % of the rise in heavy-snow days; adding winter precipitation, which rose at all 10 stations, explains about 66 %.

- Other causes checked: the Arctic Oscillation and El Niño (NOAA CPC indices) have no 35-year trend (p = 0.78 and 1.0) and add almost nothing; a warmer Sea of Japan (+1.36 °C per century, JMA), which feeds more water vapour, is the likely remainder.

- Where: cells already warmer than −3 °C in winter gained about 1.9 heavy-snow days per decade, while the cold interior below −7 °C barely changed — so towns now at −5 to −3 °C are likely next. On 178 snowy land points worldwide (5° grid) heavy snow rises where winters average −10 to −2 °C, and Hokkaido (about −4 °C) sits inside that band.

- Next decade, three estimates: today's trend extended plus two CMIP6 HighResMIP climate models (Japan's MRI-AGCM at 20 km and EC-Earth3P), applied with the same rules and checked against 1992–2026 (the models reproduce the rise in heavy snow in 15 of 20 station–model pairs, but weaker than observed). For Sapporo all three give 33–35 heavy-snow days per winter in 2027–2036 (now 31): none points to fewer. The MRI model gives a further rise at 9 of 10 stations; the European model shows no clear signal, and we say so.

- What follows: heavier roof loads, more falls on icy roads, more wet snow on power lines and trees, more wet-snow avalanches and snow-clearing accidents; a shorter snow season and less of Hokkaido's light snow. Each item is shown with our data or a cited study.

- Not yet certain: light-snow days fell significantly in 7 cells, but the chance level (6 %) is above our 5 % bar, so the app says "not yet".

- These directions agree with Japan's national assessment Climate Change in Japan 2025 (MEXT & JMA).

Why it matters

A record 1,813 people were taken to hospital after falling on Sapporo's winter roads in winter 2025, and Sapporo spends a record ~28.6 billion yen on snow in FY2026. Sapporo's worst fall days come when wet snow or rain freezes afterwards — the conditions our app flags. Winters with more heavy-snow days than the year before also had more fall injuries (r = 0.36, p = 0.03, 34 winters).

Features

- Home: a 3D Earth; click anywhere or search any place. The headline, a side view of the snowpack (1990s vs 2020s), the next 7 days and what is likely to rise or fall all follow the chosen place.

- This week's plan: a roof snow-load forecast (new-snow density from temperature) and an action calendar — grit and doorstep help for older residents the day before a fall-risk day, roof clearing after heavy snowfall, warnings for wet snow on power lines.

- World mode: outside Hokkaido, 35 winters of NASA POWER data are fetched and analysed live in the browser with the same rules (southern hemisphere: Jun–Sep).

- Snow-quality chart: one card per change — Hokkaido-wide verdict first, this town (ground station and NASA POWER) second, then "So": what to do.

- Snow timeline: one slider from 1992 (deepest snow drawn against a 170 cm person, coldest morning's wind chill, that winter's NASA MODIS snow map) to the next 7 days to 1–10 years ahead (three estimates and a map).

- Why & where: cause decomposition, other candidate causes, where snow changes most, what becomes more or less common (with sources), climate-model check, and what we cannot yet say.

- About & findings: why we made it, how to use it, the Hokkaido-wide results, falls, a trend map and open CSV/JSON data for city snow planning and research.

- Japanese, English and Korean; works on phones; installable as a web app.

How it works / tools

Python (NumPy, Pandas, Pillow, jaxa-earth) downloads and processes the data; trends are tested per winter with the Mann–Kendall test and Sen's slope, with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR, a spatially consistent shuffle test, threshold sensitivity and a detrended regression for the cause. NASA MODIS monthly snow-cover tiles from NASA GIBS are converted back to percent with the official GIBS colour map. Climate-model projections use the delta method on observations. The web app is plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript with globe.gl (three.js), Leaflet and Chart.js, hosted on GitHub Pages; world mode runs the same statistics in JavaScript.

Honesty by design

We only say "certain" when independent data agree, show "not yet" when they do not, separate what our data show from what studies and the national assessment say, and list caveats: satellites tend to under-catch snowfall, JMA snowfall is derived from depth sensors, NASA cells are ~50 km wide, the roof load counts only new snow, and the fall-risk flag is not yet validated against daily accident data.
